title: Plan, Direct and Control the Utilisation of Operational Resources

lessons.title: Planning depot resources
lessons.html:
The resources of a depot

  • Storage capacity – bins, silos, bunkers and silo bags.
  • Handling capacity – pits, elevators, conveyors, dryers, cleaners, weighbridges.
  • People – permanent and seasonal staff and contractors.
  • Energy and fuel – electricity, dryer fuel, diesel for generators and vehicles.
  • Consumables – fumigants, protectants, tarpaulins, sample bags, tickets, PPE.
  • Money – operating budget and capital for repairs and upgrades.

Capacity planning

Start with the expected intake per commodity, class and grade. Allocate bins so that each grade has space, with flexibility for unexpected grades. Example: if 30 percent of expected maize intake may be grade 2 or 3 because of a dry season, bins must be planned for that rather than assuming everything is grade 1.

Calculate peak daily handling demand and compare with the capacity of each step: weighbridge (trucks per hour), grading points (samples per hour), pits, elevators and dryers (tonnes per hour of water removal). The smallest capacity determines the depot's real throughput.

Budgeting resources

Prepare a budget for the season: labour (including overtime and seasonal contracts), electricity (based on kWh per tonne and tariffs), dryer fuel (based on expected wet grain and moisture to be removed), fumigation, maintenance and consumables. Compare with expected income from handling, storage and drying tariffs.

Maintenance planning

Schedule major maintenance before the harvest peak: elevator belts and buckets, conveyor chains, dryer burners, aeration fans, weighbridge calibration and bin repairs. Order critical spares early. Breakdowns during the intake peak are the most expensive.

Also plan consumables early. Fumigants, tarpaulins for bunkers, sample bags and PPE can have long lead times during harvest, when every depot in the region is ordering at the same time.

lessons.title: Directing and controlling resource use
lessons.html:
Directing use during the season

  • Allocate staff to shifts according to forecast truck arrivals.
  • Direct trucks with wet grain to dryers and dry grain direct to storage to balance loads.
  • Run dryers efficiently: dry to target moisture, not lower; over-drying wastes fuel and reduces grain mass sold.
  • Use aeration fans only when air conditions are suitable to save electricity.
  • Stagger large motor starts and manage peak electricity periods where tariffs penalise demand.
  • Control fumigant stock tightly; it is toxic, expensive and must be accounted for.

Monitoring and controlling

ResourceControl measure
StorageBin fill percentage, grade allocation compliance
HandlingTonnes per hour, downtime, OEE
LabourTonnes per labour hour, overtime hours
EnergykWh per tonne, dryer fuel per tonne of water removed
StockShrink percentage, book versus physical variance
BudgetActual versus budget each month

Investigate variances. If kWh per tonne rises, check for equipment running empty, worn elevator buckets, air leaks or aeration running in unsuitable conditions. If shrink is high, check weighbridge calibration, moisture meter accuracy, spillage, dust losses and security.

Security of grain and assets

Grain is valuable and theft happens. Controls include weighbridge procedures with two-person checks, CCTV, sealed out-loading trucks, access control, reconciliation of tickets and regular stock counts.

Reporting and improving

Report resource utilisation monthly with causes of variances and actions. At season end, review what resources were under- or over-used and adjust the next season's plan and budget.

Key points

  • Plan storage, handling, people, energy, consumables and budget from expected intake by grade.
  • The smallest capacity in the chain sets depot throughput.
  • Do major maintenance before the harvest peak.
  • Dry to target moisture, use aeration wisely and manage electricity demand.
  • Monitor resource KPIs, investigate variances and protect grain against theft.
